title: Where things are: the locative, the city and the home
objectives: I can name places in a city and the rooms of a home.
I can say where someone or something is with 'у', 'в' or 'на' and a noun in the locative case.
I can form the locative singular of nouns, adjectives and possessive pronouns, and explain changes such as 'апте́ка', 'в апте́ці' and 'стіл', 'на столі́'.
I can choose between 'у' and 'на' by the kind of place, and between 'у' and 'в' by euphony.
I can say who is sitting or standing where with 'сиді́ти' and 'стоя́ти'.

vocabulary.note: The locative adds '-і' to the whole word: 'у магази́ні', in the store.
The locative is 'в апте́ці': the 'к' becomes 'ц' before the ending '-і'.
The stem ends in 'к', so the locative takes '-у' and the 'к' stays: 'у ба́нку'.
Like 'банк', it takes '-у' in the locative: 'у па́рку', in the park.
The 'к' is said [ɡ], because the voiced 'з' follows it: [ʋɔɡˈzɑl]. The station takes 'на' by custom: 'на вокза́лі', at the station.
A stop is an open place, so it takes 'на', and the 'к' becomes 'ц' before '-і': 'на зупи́нці', at the stop.
The 'о' of the last syllable drops out when an ending is added, so other forms use the stem 'ри́нк-'. A market is an open place and takes 'на': 'на ри́нку'.

example.target: Сир і м’я́со є на ри́нку.
example.source: There is cheese and meat at the market.
example.source_literal: cheese and meat there-is at market

vocabulary.note: A street is an open place, so it takes 'на': 'на ву́лиці', on the street or outside. The 'ц' is soft before 'я' and 'і'.

example.source: Taras is outside on the street.

vocabulary.note: A square is an open place, so it takes 'на': 'на пло́щі'. The letter 'щ' is [ʃt͡ʃ], as in 'fresh cheese'.

example.source: The café is on the square.

vocabulary.note: 'У це́нтрі' means 'in the center' of a city, the everyday way to say 'downtown'.
Work is an activity, so it takes 'на': 'на робо́ті', at work.
The locative is 'у кварти́рі', in the apartment.
The locative is 'у кімна́ті', in the room.
The kitchen takes 'на' by custom: 'на ку́хні', in the kitchen. The 'н' is soft before 'я' and 'і'.

vocabulary.part_of_speech: feminine noun, declined like an adjective
vocabulary.note: It comes from 'ва́нна кімна́та', 'bath room', in which 'ва́нна' is an adjective. The noun 'кімна́та' was dropped and the adjective endings stayed, so the locative is 'у ва́нній'. The doubled 'н' is one long [nː].

example.source: The key is in the bathroom.

vocabulary.note: The locative is 'у бібліоте́ці': the 'к' becomes 'ц' before '-і'.
After 'й' the ending '-і' is written 'ї': 'у музе́ї', in the museum.

example.source: Today we are at the museum.

vocabulary.note: With the locative it means 'on' a surface, and 'at' or 'in' an open place, an activity or certain places: 'на столі́', 'на пло́щі', 'на робо́ті', 'на вокза́лі'.

example.source: The book is on the table.

vocabulary.note: It describes a position someone is in, not the movement of sitting down. The 'я' form changes 'д' to 'дж': 'сиджу́', 'сиди́ш', 'сидя́ть'.

example.source: I am sitting in the café.

vocabulary.note: It describes a position, and it is also the usual verb for things that stand upright in their place, such as a table, a cup or a building. Its present forms are 'стою́', 'стої́ш', 'стоя́ть'.

example.source: The cup is on the table.

dialogues.title: Where is everything here?
dialogues.context: Sam visits Oksana's neighborhood in the center of Kyiv. They are friends, so they say 'ти' to each other.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Окса́но, ти живе́ш тут, у це́нтрі?
lines.source: Oksana, do you live here, downtown?
lines.source_literal: Oksana, you live here, in center?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Так, я живу́ тут. Ось моя́ ву́лиця.
lines.source: Yes, I live here. This is my street.
lines.source_literal: Yes, I live here. Here-is my street.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Га́рна ву́лиця! А де тут апте́ка?
lines.source: What a nice street! And where's the pharmacy around here?
lines.source_literal: Nice street! And where here pharmacy?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Банк і апте́ка там, на пло́щі.
lines.source: The bank and the pharmacy are over there, on the square.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А магази́н? Я хо́чу хліб і сир.
lines.source: And a store? I want bread and cheese.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Хліб і сир є на ри́нку. Ри́нок тут, на на́шій ву́лиці.
lines.source: There's bread and cheese at the market. The market is here, on our street.
lines.source_literal: Bread and cheese there-is at market. Market here, on our street.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А твій університе́т? Він у це́нтрі?
lines.source: And your university? Is it downtown?
lines.source_literal: And your university? It in center?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Так. І бібліоте́ка там, на пло́щі. Я там сиджу́ й чита́ю.
lines.source: Yes. And the library is there too, on the square. I sit and read there.
lines.source_literal: Yes. And library there, on square. I there sit and read.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А кафе́? Де тут кафе́?
lines.source: And a café? Where's a café around here?
lines.source_literal: And café? Where here café?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Ось кафе́. Андрі́й тут працю́є.
lines.source: Here's the café. Andrii works here.
lines.source_literal: Here-is café. Andrii here works.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: До́бре! Ка́ва в кафе́, хліб на ри́нку, а кни́ги в бібліоте́ці.
lines.source: Great! Coffee at the café, bread at the market and books at the library.
lines.source_literal: Well! Coffee in café, bread at market, and books in library.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Так, Се́ме! Ти до́бре розумі́єш.
lines.source: That's right, Sam! You understand well.
lines.source_literal: Yes, Sam! You well understand.

dialogues.title: Where is everyone?
dialogues.context: Taras is out in the center of town and phones his sister Olena, who is at home. Brother and sister say 'ти' to each other.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Приві́т, Оле́но! Ти вдо́ма?
lines.source: Hi, Olena! Are you at home?
lines.source_literal: Hi, Olena! You at-home?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Приві́т! Так, я вдо́ма. А ти де?
lines.source: Hi! Yes, I'm at home. And where are you?
lines.source_literal: Hi! Yes, I at-home. And you where?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Я в це́нтрі, на пло́щі. А ма́ма й та́то?
lines.source: I'm downtown, on the square. And Mom and Dad?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Ма́ма на ку́хні. Вона́ ро́бить борщ.
lines.source: Mom is in the kitchen. She's making borscht.
lines.source_literal: Mom on kitchen. She makes borscht.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: А та́то? Він на ку́хні?
lines.source: And Dad? Is he in the kitchen?
lines.source_literal: And dad? He on kitchen?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Ні, та́то в па́рку. Він сиди́ть там і чита́є.
lines.source: No, Dad is in the park. He's sitting there reading.
lines.source_literal: No, dad in park. He sits there and reads.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: А наш кіт? Де він?
lines.source: And our cat? Where is he?
lines.source_literal: And our cat? Where he?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Кіт у ва́нній. Він сиди́ть у ва́нні!
lines.source: The cat is in the bathroom. He's sitting in the bathtub!
lines.source_literal: Cat in bathroom. He sits in bathtub!

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: У ва́нні? Чому́?
lines.source: In the bathtub? Why?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Не зна́ю. Він ду́же лю́бить ва́нну.
lines.source: I don't know. He really loves the bathtub.
lines.source_literal: Not I-know. He very loves bathtub.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: До́бре. Дя́кую, Оле́но! Бува́й!
lines.source: Okay. Thanks, Olena! Bye!
lines.source_literal: Well. I-thank, Olena! Bye!

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Бува́й!
lines.source: Bye!

dialogues.title: Where do you live?
dialogues.context: In Ukrainian class, Iryna Petrivna asks Sam where he lives and works. Teacher and student say 'ви' to each other.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Се́ме, де ви живете́? У це́нтрі?
lines.source: Sam, where do you live? Downtown?
lines.source_literal: Sam, where you live? In center?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ні, не в це́нтрі. Я живу́ в малі́й кварти́рі, але́ вона́ ду́же га́рна.
lines.source: No, not downtown. I live in a small apartment, but it's very nice.
lines.source_literal: No, not in center. I live in small apartment, but it very nice.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: А де ви працю́єте?
lines.source: And where do you work?
lines.source_literal: And where you work?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Я працю́ю вдо́ма. Мій стіл стої́ть у вели́кій кімна́ті.
lines.source: I work at home. My table is in the big room.
lines.source_literal: I work at-home. My table stands in big room.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: А ви чита́єте вдо́ма чи в бібліоте́ці?
lines.source: And do you read at home or at the library?
lines.source_literal: And you read at-home or in library?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: У бібліоте́ці. Я люблю́ там сиді́ти й чита́ти.
lines.source: At the library. I love to sit and read there.
lines.source_literal: In library. I love there to-sit and to-read.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: До́бре. Бібліоте́ка в на́шому університе́ті ду́же га́рна.
lines.source: Good. The library at our university is very beautiful.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так! А ви, Іри́но Петрі́вно? Ви живете́ в це́нтрі?
lines.source: Yes! And you, Iryna Petrivna? Do you live downtown?
lines.source_literal: Yes! And you, Iryna Petrivna? You live in center?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Так, у старо́му до́мі на пло́щі. А моя́ сестра́ живе́ у Льво́ві.
lines.source: Yes, in an old house on the square. And my sister lives in Lviv.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: У Льво́ві? Це ду́же га́рне мі́сто!
lines.source: In Lviv? It's a very beautiful city!
lines.source_literal: In Lviv? This very beautiful city!

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Так, ду́же. А за́раз ми чита́ємо.
lines.source: Yes, very. And now, let's read.
lines.source_literal: Yes, very. And now we read.

grammar.title: The locative case: saying where with 'у', 'в' and 'на'
grammar.explanation:
English says where something is with a preposition alone: 'in the store', 'at the station'. Ukrainian uses a preposition too, and it also changes the ending of the noun after it. The case that does this is the locative, in Ukrainian 'місце́вий відмі́нок', from 'мі́сце', place. It answers the question 'де?', 'where?', and unlike every other case it never appears without a preposition. In this unit the prepositions are 'у', written 'в' where euphony requires it, and 'на'. That is why the question that unit 5 gave for the locative, 'на ко́му? на чо́му?', contains a preposition.

The ending is added to the stem, the part of the word that is left when the ending of the nominative is removed. The stem of 'шко́ла' is 'шко́л-'; 'магази́н' has no ending in the nominative, so its stem is the whole word. The endings of the locative singular are:

- '-і' for feminine nouns in '-а' or '-я': 'шко́ла', 'у шко́лі'; 'ку́хня', 'на ку́хні'
- '-і' for neuter nouns in '-о': 'мі́сто', 'у мі́сті'
- '-і' for most masculine nouns: 'магази́н', 'у магази́ні'; 'вокза́л', 'на вокза́лі'; 'центр', 'у це́нтрі'
- '-ї' after 'й', because 'й' plus 'і' is the sound [ji]: 'музе́й', 'у музе́ї'
- '-у' for many masculine nouns whose stem ends in 'к', 'г' or 'х': 'парк', 'у па́рку'; 'банк', 'у ба́нку'; 'ри́нок', 'на ри́нку'

With '-у' the stem stays as it is, so 'па́рку' keeps its 'к'. Before '-і' that 'к' would change, as the spelling note of this unit shows. Some masculine nouns in 'к', 'г' or 'х' take '-і' with the change instead: 'по́тяг', train, has 'у по́тязі', in the train. The locative of each such noun is learned with it.

Nouns that never change form, such as 'кафе́' and 'меню́', stay the same after the preposition: 'у кафе́', in the café.

The adverb 'вдо́ма' and the locative 'у до́мі' need to be kept apart. The adverb 'вдо́ма' means 'at home' and is the everyday word: 'Ма́ма вдо́ма.', 'Mom is at home.' It was formed from 'в' and an old form of 'дім', so it follows the euphony of 'у' and 'в' and is written 'удо́ма' after a consonant: 'Тара́с удо́ма.' The locative of the noun, 'у до́мі', means 'in the house', the building itself.

examples.source: Taras is downtown.
They are at the museum.
Dad is at the market.
The café is in the park.
Mom is at home.
Taras is at home.

grammar.title: Adjectives and possessives in the locative, and the noun 'ва́нна'
grammar.explanation:
An adjective or a possessive pronoun before a noun copies the noun's gender, number and case, so in the locative it takes a locative ending too. In the singular there are only two endings to learn:

- '-ому' for masculine and neuter: 'у вели́кому мі́сті', 'у ново́му магази́ні'
- '-ій' for feminine: 'у вели́кій кімна́ті', 'на нові́й ву́лиці'

These endings do not depend on the noun's own ending: 'у вели́кому па́рку' has '-ому' on the adjective and '-у' on the noun, and 'у вели́кому мі́сті' has '-ому' and '-і'.

Soft-stem adjectives such as 'си́ній' keep their soft consonant, and their masculine and neuter ending is written '-ьому', because 'ьо' writes a soft consonant before 'о' (unit 3): 'у си́ньому до́мі', 'у си́ній кімна́ті'. The possessive 'ї́хній' works the same way: 'в ї́хньому до́мі', 'в ї́хній кварти́рі'.

'Наш' and 'ваш' take the same endings as 'вели́кий': 'у на́шому', 'у ва́шому'; 'у на́шій', 'у ва́шій'.

'Мій' and 'твій' have the stems 'мо[j]-' and 'тво[j]-', with 'о' in place of 'і' because the syllable is now open (unit 5). After that [j] the masculine and neuter ending is '-ему', and [j] plus 'е' is written 'є'; the feminine is [j] plus '-ій', written 'ї':

- 'мій': 'у моє́му', 'у мої́й'
- 'твій': 'у твоє́му', 'у твої́й'

'Моє́му' and 'твоє́му' are also said with the stress on the first syllable, 'мо́єму' and 'тво́єму', and both are correct. 'Його́', 'її́' and 'їх' never change, because they are genitive forms of 'він', 'вона́' and 'вони́' (unit 8): 'у його́ кімна́ті', 'в її́ кварти́рі'.

The stress of an adjective follows one rule. If the ending of the nominative is stressed, as in 'нови́й', the first vowel of the new ending takes the stress: 'ново́му', 'нові́й'. If the stem is stressed, as in 'вели́кий', the stress stays there: 'вели́кому', 'вели́кій'.

The noun 'ва́нна', bathroom, shows why these endings matter. It comes from the phrase 'ва́нна кімна́та', 'bath room', in which 'ва́нна' is an adjective describing 'кімна́та'. Speakers dropped 'кімна́та', and 'ва́нна' became a noun but kept the endings of an adjective, so its locative is 'у ва́нній', like 'у вели́кій'. A different noun with the same spelling, 'ва́нна' meaning bathtub, is an ordinary feminine noun in '-а' and takes '-і' like 'шко́ла': 'у ва́нні'.

examples.source: I live in a big city.
Oksana is at the new library.
The key is in his room.
We are in her apartment.
There is a café in our building.
The water is in the bathtub.

grammar.title: Choosing 'у' or 'на', and the verbs 'сиді́ти' and 'стоя́ти'
grammar.explanation:
'У' and 'на' both take the locative when they say where something is, and they divide places between them. Their basic meanings are close to English 'in' and 'on', and the choice depends on the kind of place:

- 'у' for the inside of a building or a room, or of an area with borders such as a park or a city center: 'у магази́ні', 'у кімна́ті', 'у па́рку', 'у це́нтрі'
- 'у' for cities and countries: 'у Ки́єві', 'у Льво́ві', 'в Украї́ні', 'у Кана́ді'
- 'на' for a surface: 'на столі́'
- 'на' for an open place: 'на пло́щі', 'на ву́лиці', 'на ри́нку', 'на зупи́нці'
- 'на' for an activity: 'на робо́ті', at work

A few places take 'на' by custom, and the choice is learned with the word. In this unit they are 'на вокза́лі', at the station, 'на по́шті', at the post office, and 'на ку́хні', in the kitchen. English has fixed choices of the same kind: people say 'on the bus' but 'in the car'. Ukraine is a country and takes the same preposition as every other country: 'в Украї́ні', in Ukraine.

'У' and 'в' are one preposition, and euphony decides which spelling is used, by the rules of unit 4:

- 'у' between consonants: 'Тара́с у ба́нку.'
- 'у' at the start of a sentence before a consonant: 'У це́нтрі є банк.'
- 'в' after a vowel before a consonant: 'Окса́на в ба́нку.'
- 'в' between vowels and at the start of a sentence before a vowel: 'Вона́ в апте́ці.', 'В університе́ті є бібліоте́ка.'
- 'у' always before 'в', 'ф', 'льв', 'св', 'тв' and 'хв': 'Ма́ма у ва́нній.', 'Вона́ у Льво́ві.'

A sentence can say where something is with no verb at all: 'Ча́шка на столі́.', 'The cup is on the table.' Ukrainian also often uses a verb of position, which says how the person or thing is placed. 'Сиді́ти' means 'to sit' in the sense 'to be sitting', and 'стоя́ти' means 'to stand' in the sense 'to be standing'. Both describe a position someone is already in, not the movement into it: 'Я сиджу́' means 'I am sitting' or 'I sit', never 'I sit down'. 'Стоя́ти' is also the usual verb for things that stand upright in their place, such as a table, a cup or a building: 'Стіл стої́ть на ку́хні.', literally 'table stands on kitchen'. English says 'is' where Ukrainian says 'stands'.

Both verbs belong to the second conjugation (unit 6) and take its endings. Their infinitives do not show this: unit 9 noted that most verbs in '-яти' are first conjugation, and so is 'розумі́ти', in '-іти'. The 'ти' forms 'сиди́ш' and 'стої́ш', with the second conjugation ending '-иш' or '-їш', are therefore learned with each verb. Two details need attention:

- 'Сиді́ти' changes 'д' to 'дж' in the 'я' form only: 'сиджу́', but 'сиди́ш' and 'сидя́ть'.
- The stem of 'стоя́ти' ends in a vowel, so its endings are written with 'ю', 'ї' and 'я': 'стою́', 'стої́ш', 'стоя́ть'.

examples.source: Sam and Oksana are on the square.
My brother is in Canada.
Taras is sitting in the café.
Olena is standing at the stop.
The table is in the kitchen.
Are you sitting in the library?

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: stem changes before '-і' and the sounds of this unit's words
grammar.explanation:
Every new word in this unit can be read with the rules of the first units, and most changes in its locative forms are old rules at work.

Before the ending '-і', the consonants 'к', 'г' and 'х' change to 'ц', 'з' and 'с', as unit 5 explained. In this unit the change appears in feminine nouns:

- 'апте́ка', 'в апте́ці'
- 'бібліоте́ка', 'у бібліоте́ці'
- 'зупи́нка', 'на зупи́нці'
- 'кни́га', 'у кни́зі'

The new consonant is soft, because it stands before 'і'. Masculine nouns such as 'парк' and 'банк' take '-у' instead and keep their 'к'.

The vowel 'і' in a closed syllable alternates with 'о' in an open one. A syllable is open when it ends in a vowel and closed when it ends in a consonant. 'Стіл' is one closed syllable, with 'і'. The ending '-і' adds a vowel, the word divides as 'сто-лі́', the first syllable is now open, and the 'о' returns: 'на столі́'. The stress also moves to the ending in this word. The same alternation gives 'дім', 'у до́мі' and 'Львів', 'у Льво́ві'. After a vowel, 'ї' alternates with 'є' in the same way: 'Ки́їв', 'у Ки́єві'.

'Ри́нок' has a fleeting vowel: a vowel that is present in the form without an ending and drops out when an ending is added. So the stem is 'ри́нк-' in every other form: 'на ри́нку'. 'Ґа́нок', porch, behaves the same way: 'на ґа́нку'.

In 'вокза́л' the 'к' stands before the voiced 'з' and is said voiced too, as [ɡ]: [ʋɔɡˈzɑl]. In Ukrainian a voiceless consonant becomes voiced before 'б', 'д', 'з', 'ж', 'г' or 'ґ', while the spelling keeps the original letter, here 'к'.

The doubled 'н' of 'ва́нна' is one long [nː], like the doubled consonant of 'життя́' (unit 3). In 'у ва́нній' and 'у ва́нні' the long 'н' is also soft, because 'і' follows it.

Four more spellings follow rules you already know:

- 'у музе́ї': 'й' plus the ending '-і' is written 'ї', which is always [ji].
- 'сиджу́': the 'я' ending of the second conjugation changes the consonant before it, as it adds 'л' after 'б' in 'роблю́' (unit 9). A stem in 'д' becomes 'дж', one sound [d͡ʒ] (unit 2), in the 'я' form only; in 'сидя́ть' the 'д' is just soft.
- 'стою́', 'стої́ш', 'стоя́ть': 'ю', 'ї' and 'я' after a vowel are [ju], [ji] and [jɑ].
- 'в' before a consonant, in the preposition and in 'вдо́ма', is said [w], the sound 'в' has at the end of a syllable. 'Окса́на в це́нтрі' is said as if the 'в' closed the syllable 'на'.

'Пло́ща' has 'щ', said [ʃt͡ʃ] as in 'fresh cheese'. In 'ку́хня' and 'ву́лиця' the 'н' and the 'ц' are soft before 'я' and 'і'.

examples.source: We are at the pharmacy.
The pencil is on the table.
We are in Lviv.
Sam is at the railway station.
The museum is in Kyiv.
I am sitting on the porch.

culture.title: City life and the Ukrainian apartment
culture.text:
Most people in Ukrainian cities live in apartments, 'кварти́ри', in buildings of several floors. An apartment is described by the number of its rooms, and the kitchen and the bathroom are not counted, so an apartment with two rooms, a kitchen and a bathroom is called a two-room apartment. In many apartments the toilet is in a small room of its own, next to the bathroom, 'ва́нна', which holds the bathtub and the sink.

The kitchen, 'ку́хня', is the heart of an apartment. Family and guests often sit 'на ку́хні' rather than in the main room, drinking tea and talking late into the evening, and long conversations at the kitchen table are a familiar part of Ukrainian life.

A Ukrainian city has a center, 'центр', its old and busy downtown, usually built around a main square, 'пло́ща'. In Kyiv the best known is Independence Square, which Kyivans call the Maidan. In Lviv the old center surrounds a square called 'пло́ща Ри́нок', Market Square, because markets were held there for centuries. The name stays as it is after the noun 'пло́ща', so people arrange to meet 'на пло́щі Ри́нок'.

Three other places belong to everyday city life:

- Markets, 'ри́нки', where many people buy fresh meat, cheese, vegetables and fruit from the farms around the city.
- Pharmacies, 'апте́ки', found on almost every street and marked by a green cross.
- The railway station, 'вокза́л'. Trains are the usual way to travel between Ukrainian cities, and the main station of a big city is busy day and night.

exercises.explanation: 'Апте́ка' is a pharmacy. The library is 'бібліоте́ка', the railway station 'вокза́л' and the bank 'банк'.

exercises.prompt: Match the Ukrainian with the English
Which question does a noun in the locative answer?
exercises.explanation: The locative says where someone or something is, so it answers 'де?', 'where?'.
Most masculine nouns add '-і' in the locative: 'магази́н', 'у магази́ні'.

exercises.prompt: Match each phrase with its meaning
Why does 'парк' take the ending '-у' in 'у па́рку'?
choices: Many masculine nouns whose stem ends in 'к', 'г' or 'х' take '-у'
exercises.explanation: Many masculine nouns with a stem in 'к', 'г' or 'х' take '-у' in the locative, which keeps the stem unchanged: 'у па́рку', 'у ба́нку', 'на ри́нку'.

exercises.hint_source: The pen is on the table.
exercises.explanation: The locative of 'стіл' adds '-і'. The ending opens the syllable, so the 'і' of 'стіл' becomes 'о': 'на столі́'.
A feminine noun in '-а' takes '-і', and before '-і' the 'к' becomes 'ц': 'апте́ка', 'в апте́ці'.

exercises.prompt: In 'бібліоте́ка', 'у бібліоте́ці', why is the 'к' replaced by 'ц'?
choices: The stress moves to the ending
exercises.explanation: Before the ending '-і', 'к', 'г' and 'х' become 'ц', 'з' and 'с'. The stress of 'бібліоте́ці' stays where it was.

choices: The stress always falls on an 'о'
The ending opens the syllable, and 'і' in a closed syllable alternates with 'о' in an open one
exercises.explanation: 'Стіл' is one closed syllable. With the ending '-і' the word divides as 'сто-лі́', the first syllable is open, and the 'о' returns.

choices: We are sitting at the stop.
We are standing on the square.
We are standing at the stop.
A position someone is in: being seated
exercises.explanation: 'Сиді́ти' means 'to be sitting', a position held. 'Я сиджу́' is 'I am sitting', never 'I sit down'.

exercises.hint_source: I am sitting in the kitchen.
exercises.explanation: The 'я' form of 'сиді́ти' changes 'д' to 'дж': 'сиджу́'.

exercises.hint_source: They are standing at the railway station.
exercises.explanation: 'Стоя́ти' is a second conjugation verb whose stem ends in a vowel, so the 'вони́' form is 'стоя́ть'.

exercises.prompt: Why is it 'на ку́хні' but 'у кімна́ті'?
choices: 'Ку́хня' takes 'на' by custom, and the choice is learned with the word
A kitchen is an open place, like a square
exercises.explanation: A room is an enclosed space and takes 'у'. 'Ку́хня' is one of the few places that take 'на' by custom, like 'вокза́л' and 'по́шта'.
A market is an open place, so it takes 'на'.

exercises.prompt: In 'Окса́на в ба́нку', why is the preposition written 'в'?
choices: It comes after a vowel and before a consonant
exercises.explanation: By the euphony rules, 'в' is used after a vowel before a consonant. After a consonant, as in 'Тара́с у ба́нку', the preposition is 'у'.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'in my apartment'?
exercises.explanation: 'Мій' becomes 'мої́й' before a feminine noun in the locative. 'Твої́й' is 'your', of 'ти'; 'на́шій' is 'our'; 'ва́шій' is 'your', of 'ви'.

exercises.hint_source: They live in a big city.
exercises.explanation: 'Мі́сто' is neuter, so the adjective takes '-ому' in the locative. The stem of 'вели́кий' is stressed, so the stress stays there.

exercises.hint_source: The key is in my room.
exercises.explanation: 'Кімна́та' is feminine, so 'мій' takes the feminine locative 'мої́й'.

exercises.prompt: Why is the locative of 'ва́нна', bathroom, 'у ва́нній'?
choices: It is a noun that kept the adjective endings of 'ва́нна кімна́та'
exercises.explanation: 'Ва́нна', bathroom, was the adjective in 'ва́нна кімна́та'. 'Кімна́та' was dropped, and the noun kept the adjective endings, so it takes '-ій' like 'у вели́кій'.
'Ва́нна', bathroom, declines like an adjective, so the locative is 'ва́нній'. The preposition is 'у', not 'в', because 'у' is always used before 'в'.

exercises.prompt: In the first dialogue, where does Oksana say there is bread and cheese?
exercises.explanation: Oksana says 'Хліб і сир є на ри́нку.', 'There's bread and cheese at the market.'

exercises.prompt: In the phone call between Taras and Olena, where is the cat sitting?
exercises.explanation: Olena says 'Він сиди́ть у ва́нні!', 'He's sitting in the bathtub!' 'Ва́нні' is the locative of 'ва́нна', bathtub, while 'ва́нній' is the locative of 'ва́нна', bathroom.

exercises.prompt: In the class dialogue, where does Iryna Petrivna's sister live?
exercises.explanation: Iryna Petrivna says 'А моя́ сестра́ живе́ у Льво́ві.', 'And my sister lives in Lviv.'

exercises.hint_source: The library is at the university.

exercises.prompt_source: The pharmacy is on the square.
The glass is on the table.
Mom and Dad are at home.
My sister lives in a big city.

exercises.explanation: A city center is an area with borders, so it takes 'у', and 'центр' adds '-і'. After the consonant of 'банк' the preposition is 'у'.

exercises.prompt_source: My key is in the kitchen.
exercises.explanation: 'Ку́хня' takes 'на' by custom, and the feminine '-я' becomes '-і'.
A country takes 'у', spelled 'в' here because a vowel comes before and after it. 'Украї́на' changes '-а' to '-і'.

exercises.prompt_source: Taras is sitting in the park.
exercises.explanation: 'Сиди́ть' is the 'він' form of 'сиді́ти'. 'Парк' takes '-у' in the locative, and after a consonant the preposition is 'у'.
